definition: The number of distinct drawings per second (DPS) a hold-density choice (ones/twos/threes/...) produces must not drop so low, relative to a short action's own total frame count, that too few distinct poses remain to read the action at all.
purpose: Prevent a fixed hold-density habit (e.g. always animating on twos) from silently under-serving an action too short to afford it.
visible_effect: A very short action animated at a hold density chosen for longer actions shows too few distinct poses in sequence, reading as an incomplete or jerky approximation of the intended motion rather than a smooth one.
psychological_or_gameplay_effect: The action reads as "strange" or under-drawn — not because the individual poses are wrong, but because there are too few of them for the eye to reconstruct the intended motion.
physical_interpretation: FPS (the fixed display rate) sets a hard ceiling on DPS (how many distinct drawings can appear per second); a hold-density choice divides that ceiling down, and a short action has too few total frames for a coarse division to leave enough poses behind.
use_cases: a fast or very short action (the video's own example: a five-frame run cycle) — favor ones, or as few frames held per pose as the budget allows
any action whose total frame count is already close to the minimum number of poses the eye needs to read it
non_use_cases: a longer action with frames to spare, where twos or threes remain the more economical default (per the existing pose-hold-density guidance from W01 video 1)
a style that deliberately wants a choppy, under-posed look — here a sparse pose count is the intended effect rather than a defect
interactions: Pose hold density (W01 video 1) — this is the specific breaking case at the SHORT end of that same ones/twos/threes dial: hold density has to shrink as available frame count shrinks
Startup frame budget (W01 video 2) — the genre-level fast-action case (a roughly 3-frame fighting-game hit) is exactly the regime this entry's floor applies to hardest
Timing — DPS is a direct, computable function of an action's own frame count and the declared hold density, not a separate quantity
cadence_representation: Directly computable from data this build already has: an item's key density over a frame range (`ai/motion.js keyDensity`) already reports how many distinct keys exist in a span; nothing currently compares that count against the span's own duration to flag an under-posed short action, but both numbers this check would need already exist.
control_surface: `analyze_motion` (`keyDensity`) reports the raw count; no tool currently flags a shortfall against the action's own duration.
detection_and_measurement_methods: `ai/motion.js keyDensity` measures distinct keys over a frame range directly — a real, existing measurement this check could be built from without any new instrumentation.
generation_or_modification_methods: None — this is a diagnostic check, not an edit; fixing a flagged shortfall means adding poses, which no strategy in `ai/plan.js` can do (no strategy may add a key).
failure_modes: defaulting to twos or threes out of habit on an action too short to afford it, producing the exact under-posed "only three poses for a run cycle" case the video names directly
flagging a deliberately sparse, stylized action as a defect when the low pose count was the intended look
roblox_considerations: None specific — a pure frame-count/pose-count relationship independent of the target engine.
examples: a five-frame run cycle animated on twos yields poses only on frames one, three and five — three poses total, described as looking "strange" (video @ 4:20–4:29)
the same five frames animated on ones yields five distinct poses, enough to read the run cycle naturally (video @ 4:29–4:33)
